title: Nigga, the Peace Table Has to Stand Up
subtitle: Puzzles, mechanisms, creative toys and retro desktop diversions

opening.title: The Battle of the Unassembled Stage
paragraphs: The mechanism inside my enormous box was a curtain opener with no curtain, a revolving stand with no assigned purpose, and a gold lever so impressive it distracted me from both omissions.
Rae put the delivery sheet on the table. "Which thing does the useful thing?"
I pointed at the lever.
She lifted it. Nothing happened anywhere else.
Tank nodded. "Portable authority, nigga."

Our venue annex was settled. People knew where the rooms were, the quiet space had a working lamp, and Velvet's dressing area no longer doubled as a shortcut for my sense of symmetry. All that remained was to build a ceremony capable of holding the people, the paper, the costumes, and my deteriorating confidence without collapsing under any of them.
I had prepared for this task by ordering objects.

Mika had prepared by measuring. This gave them an unfair advantage the moment we began. They placed their tiny hotel model on a clear patch of table, laid out the agreed route, and asked us to stop adding towers until the actual furniture worked.

Kit, the white butch librarian, carried the lighting plan under one arm and searched for her glasses with the other hand. They were in her jacket pocket. Remy discovered them while looking for the microphone clip, received a grateful smile, and ruined it with a pun about seeing eye to eye. Kit laughed anyway, which encouraged him beyond the interests of the room.

Velvet arrived wearing half her performance costume and carrying the other half in a bag large enough to contain a small successful business. She wanted a clear turn beside the stage, a usable mirror, and the fee we had already agreed. Her budget instincts were sharper than my scissors, and considerably more likely to cut something.

Rae wanted the signing table to stand still. This had become her recurring demand because I had repeatedly purchased things that photographed better than they supported elbows. Nia wanted that table near the room, where people could speak without being exhibited like auction lots. She also wanted to ask Rae about the dance, but every time she approached, somebody handed her another page written in my decorative language.

Auntie June and Dez took their chairs near the rehearsal area. June wore the posture of a retired bus driver who could still tell when somebody had parked badly from across a room. Dez wore June's old jacket, repaired so carefully that its disputed ownership had survived longer than many actual institutions.

Between them lay the Blue Comet rental invoice. The peace terms were on its back. June had signed the front and Dez the back, an arrangement that had supported fifty-nine years of each declaring the other's signature absent. I had initially treated this as a tragedy of diplomacy. Shawna said it sounded like two women who enjoyed having an excuse to bring up the same night.

The first Great Butch versus Stud War belonged to our invented 1967 social club history, complete with contradictory jukebox accounts and an unreasonable quantity of emotional investment in one borrowed jacket. The second had reached the stage-equipment phase. Nobody's dignity required a vote. My purchases, unfortunately, required several.

I proposed raising the signing table on a platform beneath the illuminated portrait. Rae sat at the table and asked me to hand her the pen. I had to walk around a vase, a costume rack, and the unconnected lever to reach her.
"Nigga," she said, "we have discovered the problem."
Mika moved the vase. Kit moved the rack. I held the lever because nobody had yet found it a job. Shawna put a small ordinary pen in my other hand and guided me back along the clear route.
"Try this version."
I handed the pen to Rae. She wrote a test word, pushed gently against the table, and looked up. It wobbled.
Tank took the lever from me. For one terrible second I thought he had discovered its purpose. Then he set it aside and helped Rae inspect the legs.
The war had finally found its first objective: a table that could survive somebody agreeing with somebody else.

interludes.title: Dez Refused to Let the Jacket Lose on a Technicality
paragraphs: The costume rehearsal stopped when June noticed a loose thread at Dez's cuff. She reached for it. Dez caught her wrist gently.
"Leave it. You'll make it worse."
"I drove a bus full of people through winter. I can manage a thread."
"That's why I never let the bus hem my clothes."

Rae laughed into her drink. Nia tried not to, failed, and ended up holding the glass while Rae found a small sewing kit. Dez accepted the kit with the calm of somebody returning to familiar tools. June stayed beside her despite having several strong opinions about being supervised.

The jacket lay across both their knees. It had belonged to June first. It had spent enough time with Dez that every repair was also a small account of where it had been. Neither woman needed me to explain this, so naturally I began.
Shawna put a sandwich in my mouth.

Dez repaired the cuff. June held the little lamp at a useful angle without commenting on the appointment. Velvet came over to inspect the work and asked whether Dez would look at a loose fastening on her costume.
"For you, yes."
I offered to make the work an official heritage demonstration. Dez told me to finish chewing.

The repairs were small, exact, and almost invisible when done. They made the clothes behave better without making their wearers into examples of anything. Remy tried his stage turn nearby. Kit adjusted the light and accidentally directed it into my eyes, which everybody regarded as an acceptable temporary arrangement.
When Dez handed the jacket back to June, the room went quiet for one beat. June inspected the cuff, nodded, and helped Dez put it on again.
"There," she said.
"About time you returned it," Dez answered.
The old argument resumed before I could declare peace. Nia laughed properly this time, and Rae looked at her as if the sound had improved the room.
Mika called us back to the rehearsal route. The table still needed checking, the curtain still needed its final position, and the jacket had won the right to keep going without a plaque.

interludes.title: The Camera Did Not Get to Name Everybody
paragraphs: The photographer arrived during the costume check and asked where he should put the men.
Remy raised one hand. Tank raised a bread roll. I stepped into the best light on instinct.
The photographer pointed at Velvet, Kit, and Rae.
"Also you three. The masculine side of the group."
Velvet looked down at her silver costume, then back at him.
"Baby, if this is your idea of masculine, I need to see what you wore to work yesterday."

His name was Owen. He was an adult gay man hired by the hotel, which he told us immediately, as if the information might excuse the photograph before he took it. It did not make him a villain. It also did not arrange anybody's feet.
"I meant the presentation," he said.
"Then ask about the picture you want," Remy said. "Don't assign people a whole life to get a balanced triangle."
I offered to form the triangle around myself. Shawna moved me two feet to the left and improved the conversation.

Owen lowered the camera and claimed he had meant to separate sharp tailoring from flowing costumes. Velvet looked down at the dress he had put on the tailored side. Even his excuse needed rearranging.

Kit considered the new proposal. She was willing to stand beside the silver costume. Rae wanted to remain beside Nia. Velvet wanted the light slightly higher. Remy wanted his name used when he was not performing.
These requests did not require a tribunal. Owen listened, adjusted, and began again.

The fees were already protected by the earlier budget argument. I thought that meant the photograph would be easy. Then the hotel's sponsorship coordinator arrived with an opinion nobody had purchased.

Martin was an adult straight man with a cheerful voice and the confidence of somebody accustomed to explaining what would appeal to everyone. He asked whether the photograph could look a little less like a drag show and more like a coalition.
Velvet folded one arm across the other.
"What do you think a coalition looks like?"
"A broader group."
"You're looking at one."
He said he meant the general public. Rae asked which people in the room had ceased to be members of it when they put their clothes on.

I enjoyed that question so much I nearly repeated it into the microphone. Nia took the microphone off its stand and passed it to Remy before I could turn somebody else's irritation into my own grand moment.
Martin tried to clarify. He wanted the picture to look welcoming. The glitter, the posture, the deliberate styling might appear confrontational to some guests.
Kit glanced at Rae. This time she did not rush to explain Rae's expression for her.
Rae said, "Which posture?"
Martin looked at the camera rather than at her. "I'm not singling anybody out."
"You're already choosing who counts as the public. Tell us who gets left out."
The room became quiet. Owen set his camera on the table.

Martin admitted that he had asked Rae to soften her expression during an earlier test shot. He had described Kit's equally serious face as strong. Hearing the two instructions together embarrassed him more effectively than anything I could have purchased.
Rae did not smile to reward the admission.
"I don't need to perform friendly twice as hard so your brochure can feel relaxed."
Kit looked at her own test image. "And I don't want my picture used as the reasonable version of hers."
June gave a short approving noise from the front row. Then she told both younger women that neither was required to keep a serious expression out of principle if something was funny.
"Nigga, don't let the photographer steal your laugh just because you won't sell it."
Rae laughed at that, which was June's joke earning a response, not Martin's request finally being obeyed.

Owen asked whether everyone wanted a break before the group photograph. Rae said yes. Velvet said she wanted her individual stage pictures first, under the terms already agreed. Kit went to find her glasses. Remy tested the microphone with a joke so bad Martin laughed before remembering he was in trouble.
"You're allowed," Remy told him. "The joke's terrible for everybody."
During the break, Kit sat beside Velvet and asked whether she got tired of having every elaborate outfit treated as a declaration about her entire existence.
Velvet removed one earring. "Sometimes I want it to be a declaration. Sometimes I want you to notice I paid somebody to sew the damn hem."
"How do people know which?"
"They can ask a question smaller than what are you."

Velvet remembered one gay club booking where a man who called her family had then asked her to work for less. Another man at the same club had quietly fixed the payment before the show. She liked remembering both, especially because neither account let anybody use belonging as a discount code.

Kit nodded. She talked about enjoying a good jacket without wanting it interpreted as either a failure to be a woman or a promise to behave like a man. Rae joined them but did not simply echo her. She liked the word stud. It connected to a Black lesbian world she recognized, to people and style and ways of carrying herself that were not available for anybody else's casual relabeling.
"I like what we recognise in each other. I don't want to make your word mine," Kit said.
"Good. I like what we share," Rae said. "I'm still going to tell you when you get me wrong."
June leaned forward. "And leave room for an old Black butch. Some of us were here before your categories got assigned hotel rooms."
Dez touched her sleeve. "You were here before the chairs."
"Still more comfortable than that first jukebox stool."
The room laughed, then returned to the conversation without making either veteran an honorary textbook.

Remy unfastened the small crown from his costume. As King Receipts he could make himself grander, louder, and deliberately ridiculous. As Remy he wanted his date to know he was nervous about the flowers.
"I don't stop being me when the crown comes off," he said. "I just stop charging the room interest."
Velvet snorted. "Keep that one. It almost worked."
Nia asked Rae whether she liked being seen as protective. Rae considered the question.
"Sometimes. When I choose it. I like taking care of people. I also like somebody noticing I'm tired before handing me another box."
Nia set down the box she had been about to offer.
"Oh."
"That one was funny."

They smiled, but the question stayed useful. Caring could be pleasure. It could also become a job people assigned by looking at a body, a jacket, a voice, or the person standing beside it. Rae did not want her tenderness denied. She wanted the right to decide what she did with it.

Kit admitted that she sometimes enjoyed being read as competent before she had earned it. The temptation was especially strong when an event already treated her confidence as less alarming than Rae's. She could not fix that by pretending nobody noticed race, or by claiming Rae's experiences as another version of her own.
"I can stop accepting the comparison as a compliment," she said.
"That's a start," Rae answered. "It doesn't require me to grade the rest of your life."

Owen returned and asked whether they wanted the arrangement kept or changed. He did not call the room boys, girls, masculine, feminine, or brave. He used names. Martin stayed beside him and listened while Mika explained what the picture was for: a record of this evening, not proof that every person outside it would approve.

Mika set one further condition: each person could approve the photograph and caption before the hotel posted either. Nia added that declining the picture would not mean declining the coalition. Martin wrote that down. It was a smaller promise than universal welcome, and one he could actually keep.
I offered to put a political declaration beneath the photograph.
Nia asked which declaration.
"Something powerful."
"Then know what you mean before ordering the lettering."
Shawna rescued me with a more demanding assignment: stand beside her and look as if I wanted to be there.

We made the picture with Rae next to Nia, Kit near Velvet, Remy holding his crown rather than wearing it, and June and Dez comfortably seated. Some people smiled. Some did not. The photographer took more than one image so nobody had to become the single official expression of an identity.
Afterward, Velvet put her earring back on and asked Owen for the stage light she had originally requested. He adjusted it without explaining himself again.
"Nigga," she said to me, "now watch the entrance."
She stepped through the curtain. The room belonged to her for that moment because she knew exactly what she was doing, and because the rest of us finally had the sense to look.

interludes.title: The Pen Was Tested on Paper That Did Not Bind Anybody
paragraphs: We reached the rehearsal where everything looked ready enough to tempt me into a premature conclusion. The curtain worked. The light worked. Remy's microphone no longer produced a sound like a distressed kitchen appliance.
I picked up the charter.
Nia put a blank sheet beneath my hand.
"Practice paper."
"Nigga, I know what paper is."
"Then you'll appreciate the distinction."

Rae sat at the table and wrote her name. The pen worked, the table stayed still, and the vase remained far enough away to contribute nothing except looking like a vase. Kit sat next, then Velvet, who signed her stage name with an extravagant sweep that cost no one an extra chair.
Remy drew a small crown. Mika sketched a tiny hotel. Tank wrote DINNER and underlined it twice.

June examined both sides of the blank sheet before writing anything. Dez watched her, then turned the sheet over with a look that made fifty-nine years of Blue Comet argument briefly visible in one wrist movement.
"We can use the same side this time," she said.
June laughed. She did not pick up the actual agreement. Neither did Dez. The moment was a possibility, not a settlement I had permission to announce.
Shawna drew a small heart on the practice page and handed me the pen. I started writing an extravagant dedication. She tapped the little space beside her heart.
"Here."
I wrote our initials, which proved sufficient for the task.

Mika gathered the practice sheets and left the real charter untouched in its tray. Nia still wanted to check the final wording. People still had their own conversations to finish. The room could be ready without requiring everybody inside it to move at the same speed.

I asked whether we could at least have a photograph of the successful rehearsal. Velvet said yes, after she adjusted one earring. Remy waited. Kit moved the lamp. For once, the picture happened when the people were ready instead of when I declared the light historically significant.

ending.title: The Stage Could Hold the Peace, If We Ever Finished Talking
paragraphs: At the final equipment check, the table stood still. I pressed one corner to confirm this personally, then another because I disliked being excluded from a successful test.
Rae watched me. "You can stop trying to make it interesting."

The curtain opened. Velvet stepped through, made her turn, and reached the microphone with her costume intact. Remy followed at the agreed distance, delivered one deliberately terrible fanfare, and bowed before the joke became an endurance event. Kit found the light flattering enough to defend publicly.

Mika checked the route from the quiet room. June took it at her own pace. Dez walked beside her with the Blue Comet invoice safely inside her bag. They could reach the table without climbing, squeezing past my portrait, or listening to an explanatory recording about why the route was grand.
Mercedes played a few notes. Porsche listened from the seat she had chosen. Tank set down the snack tray where it could be reached, and Rosa immediately proved the placement successful.
"Nigga," I said, "look what we built."
Shawna looked at the room. Then she looked at me.
"Yes. We did."

The word we landed properly that time. It included the hotel workers, the people who measured, the people who asked for a chair, the people who cut a bad idea, and the people whose costume needed more room than my first sketch allowed. It also included me, though not always in the position I had drawn for myself.
I picked up the lever one last time. Remy asked whether I wanted it in the museum or the return box.
"The return box."
Tank put a hand to his chest as if witnessing a miracle. I threatened to order something just to restore his understanding of the world. He handed me a plate before I could act.

The new charter remained unsigned. Its final wording belonged to the next conversations, including matters too personal for my microphone. Nia crossed the room to Rae with no page in her hand. Rae set down the toolkit. Whatever she asked next was quiet enough that neither I nor the ceremony needed to own it.

June and Dez sat beside the finished stage. One remembered the first Blue Comet song; the other remembered the last. Mercedes asked them to hum both. The versions disagreed, but she found a few notes that let them begin together.
I almost announced the second war over. Shawna kissed the beginning of the announcement away.
"Not yet."
"Then what now?"
She took my hand and led me toward the seats. "Let them talk. Sit with me."
The stage was ready. The paper could wait. I sat down before somebody found another useful thing for me to carry, and discovered that this, too, counted as contributing to the peace.

games.title: Baba Is You
games.case_title: HOST IS OPTIONAL Was an Act of War
scene: Baba Is You had me thinking about moveable rules, which was unfortunate because Rae was already rearranging the magnetic words on my ceremony board.
I had written HOST IS ESSENTIAL. She changed it to HOST IS SEATED.
"Nigga, that's constitutional vandalism."
Kit changed STAGE IS GRAND to STAGE IS CLEAR. Velvet added PAID beside SHOW and folded her arms until I acknowledged the amendment.
Auntie June examined the board. She said the Blue Comet jukebox dispute had begun with people treating their own rules as sacred. Dez said it had begun with June playing the same song four times.
"Because it was good."
"Because you had all the quarters."
Remy moved the word SHARED beside MICROPHONE. The resulting sentence was ugly but useful. I put OPTIONAL beside my speech as a generous gesture, then tried to remove it when everyone applauded.
Shawna kept her hand over the magnet. Nigga, my wife had discovered a very small way to hold executive power.
games.pleasure: Baba Is You turns the rules of a puzzle into objects you can move. A short arrangement of words can transform what a wall, flag or character does. The appeal is the surprise of realizing that the rule you assumed was fixed is actually the thing to manipulate.
games.burden: The small number of movement actions should not be confused with easy reasoning. The developer describes a large collection of increasingly inventive rule interactions. Reading the words, predicting consequences and revising a plan can become demanding. Check the exact movement, undo and restart controls rather than assuming they are comfortable because the board is compact.
games.first: Try an introductory level and deliberately move one rule word. Observe what changes before attempting a long solution or consulting an entire set of hints.
games.ruling: The ceremony board keeps shared equipment and an optional host speech. June and Dez dispute the historical jukebox allocation, while Shawna guards the magnet that makes the present tolerable.
games.source_note: Exact-title developer/publisher Steam description inspected for premise and edition. Fit and first trial are editorial suggestions. Controls, timing and comfort remain bounded by the explicit checks in the card; no complete playthrough performed.
games.quick_pitch: Discover puzzles where moving the words changes the rules, if a small action leading to a big conceptual surprise appeals.
games.what_you_do: Move around compact boards, push rule words into new arrangements and observe how the changed rules affect the puzzle.
games.watch_for: The simple movement system supports difficult reasoning; verify movement repeat, undo and exact controls before choosing it.

games.title: Patrick's Parabox
games.case_title: The Table Was Inside the Table's Box
scene: Patrick's Parabox put boxes inside boxes while the hotel delivered our signing furniture in a crate that seemed to contain another crate.
Mika opened the first. Tank opened the second. I announced that anticipation increased the ceremony's value.
Rae found a tiny model table inside the third.
"Nigga, you ordered the display sample."
I examined the invoice. The scale measurement had looked like a decorative fraction.
Velvet sat the miniature table on her palm and asked whether the coalition planned to sign with individual eyelashes. Remy produced a pencil nub and offered a suitably modest fanfare.
Mika was delighted. They added the model to their hotel collection, then borrowed a full-size table from the lounge. Rae checked its legs. Kit arranged the chairs around it.
The small table cost too much to throw away, so Shawna placed it beside my enormous receipt. In that arrangement, at least, the proportions accurately represented my evening.
games.pleasure: Patrick's Parabox explores boxes that contain other boxes, including recursive arrangements. The repeated act of pushing gains new meaning as the space folds into itself. Its interest is in discovering how a small set of relationships can support surprisingly rich puzzles.
games.burden: The current Steam listing declares play without timed input and keyboard-only support. Spatial nesting can still require holding several relationships in mind even when the controls are limited. Verify key repeat, undo and any zoom behavior in the actual version. There is little conventional character story to carry the experience if the recursive logic itself does not appeal.
games.first: Play the earliest introduction to entering and leaving a box. Explain one relationship aloud if useful, then try a move that tests that explanation.
games.ruling: The borrowed table receives the actual chairs, while Mika keeps the expensive miniature. My receipt becomes a scale reference for the distance between anticipation and reading the purchase description.
games.source_note: Exact Steam developer description supports premise. Current developer declarations include Playable without Timed Input and Keyboard Only Option. Physical comfort, held inputs and reasoning load still need their stated checks; this is not a hands-on completion test.
games.quick_pitch: Explore boxes within boxes, if discovering how nested spaces fit together sounds more interesting than following a conventional character story.
games.what_you_do: Move pieces through recursive box arrangements, reconsider the spatial relationships and try new paths through the compact puzzle.
games.watch_for: The developer declares untimed input, but nested relationships can create substantial reasoning and memory demands.

games.title: Stephen's Sausage Roll
games.case_title: The Sausage Had a Seating Preference
scene: Stephen's Sausage Roll made the food layout look like an exact spatial problem, which Rae took as permission to intervene in the catering arrangement.
The sausages were under a hot lamp. The bread was across the table. The plates sat behind a vase taller than Remy.
"Nigga, who designed this, a person who hates wrists?"
I admitted choosing the vase. It was shaped like a victory flame.

Dez rotated the platter and moved the bread beside it. June shifted the plates. They performed this small cooperation without acknowledging its diplomatic significance, so I immediately ruined it by announcing the historic moment.
June put a plate in my hand.
"Be historic over there."
Rae used the freed space for a clear serving route. Velvet approached, assembled dinner without touching the victory flame, and declared the arrangement fit for performers of international stature.
Tank asked whether international stature wanted her second sausage. She moved her plate. Negotiations remained rigorous.
games.pleasure: Stephen's Sausage Roll is a compact three-dimensional puzzle game built around unusually exact spatial problems. Its appeal is the satisfaction of understanding a small arrangement deeply enough to make it work. It belongs on the reasoning shelf for someone who enjoys a stubborn little mechanism more than an expansive story.
games.burden: The inspected primary storefront supplies very little detailed control information, so this card does not certify timing, holds or the full interaction set. The title's cheerful food premise should not imply easy puzzles. Treat both input comfort and the amount of planning as questions for an early trial, with no expectation of quick completion.
games.first: Inspect the first small puzzle and test a single movement. If the rules interest you, try one hypothesis; if they merely irritate, leave the plate unfinished.
games.ruling: The serving arrangement prioritizes reachable plates and actual food. June and Dez decline a commemorative announcement, while Velvet retains both sausages under a clear and vigorously defended claim.
games.source_note: Exact-game Steam description is very brief ('A simple 3d puzzle game'); source supports identity and basic genre, not detailed control or difficulty certification. Scene is original fiction. Specific input and full-game timing remain to be checked.
games.quick_pitch: Work through compact spatial puzzles built around a comic cooking premise, if figuring out a demanding arrangement sounds satisfying.
games.what_you_do: Inspect the puzzle space, move through its arrangement and test how your actions change the problem in front of you.
games.watch_for: The primary description is brief; controls and full-game timing remain unresolved, and the reasoning can be demanding.

games.title: Snakebird
games.case_title: The Feather Boa Outgrew the Floor Plan
scene: Snakebird's changing shape suggested a problem Velvet had already brought into the room: every time she improved her costume, it occupied another chair.
Her feather boa crossed the model map like a glamorous river.
Mika lifted one end. Rae moved the snack bowl away from the other. Remy said the outfit now required its own entrance music and a turning permit.
"Nigga, it's called presence," Velvet said.
Kit measured the proposed stage passage with a ribbon. Velvet tried the turn, caught a feather on my portrait stand, and removed the portrait without consulting its subject.
The turn worked.
I argued that the obstruction had been artistically important. Velvet wrapped the boa around my shoulders and invited me to demonstrate a better route.
I became trapped between two chairs while everybody watched. Shawna freed one end, kissed my cheek, and asked whether presence wanted help.
Presence accepted. The stage passage became wider, and my portrait began another involuntary tour of the building.
games.pleasure: Snakebird makes the length and shape of its fruit-eating creatures central to spatial puzzles. What looks like a small comic animal becomes a tool for crossing, supporting and arranging a route. The attraction is the way a simple change in body length changes the whole problem.
games.burden: The developer explicitly calls the game deceptively challenging. A friendly drawing and a small board should not be sold as easy reasoning. Check directional input, switching between creatures and recovery from mistakes. The card does not establish universal no-timing behavior from genre alone; its strongest case is for a player who enjoys concentrated spatial experimentation.
games.first: Try the earliest fruit-and-exit arrangement. Notice what the new length permits before attempting to plan several moves ahead.
games.ruling: The costume gets a tested turning space and the portrait gets relocated. Presence may request assistance without surrendering glamour, a provision I endorse after briefly becoming part of the furniture.
games.source_note: Exact-title developer/publisher Steam description inspected for premise and edition. Fit and first trial are editorial suggestions. Controls, timing and comfort remain bounded by the explicit checks in the card; no complete playthrough performed.
games.quick_pitch: Guide an awkward growing creature through spatial puzzles, if planning around its shape sounds like an enjoyable challenge to explore.
games.what_you_do: Move the creature through a puzzle arrangement and account for how its changing shape affects the possible route.
games.watch_for: The developer calls the puzzles challenging; colorful creatures and limited controls do not establish easy reasoning.

games.title: Snakebird Primer
games.case_title: The Introductory Boa Saved My Marriage
scene: After the full feather arrangement defeated me, Kit proposed a smaller rehearsal costume. Snakebird Primer was on the screen, offering a gentler introduction to its own spatial ideas.
Velvet selected a short scarf and draped it around my shoulders.
"Training wheels, nigga."
I strode toward the stage, turned cleanly, and bowed. Remy played a fanfare so ridiculous I forgot to be offended. Shawna applauded with actual affection rather than the earlier rescue expression.
June said Dez had once practiced an entrance through a doorway with a jacket over one shoulder. Dez said the jacket had belonged to June, who had invented the rehearsal story to get it back.
"Did it work?" Rae asked.
"Ask the jacket," June said.
Velvet took the scarf and showed me how one small movement could look deliberate. No collision. No rented spotlight. I tried again.
Shawna crooked a finger from the front row. The rehearsal suddenly had a destination that made my extravagant entrance budget seem very poorly targeted.
games.pleasure: Snakebird Primer is a separate set of puzzles designed as a more approachable introduction to Snakebird's spatial ideas. The developer explicitly contrasts its easier island with the original game's serious challenges. It can be a useful place to discover whether moving and shaping these creatures is pleasurable before choosing the harder title.
games.burden: Easier is a comparison, not a personal guarantee. Directional movement, visual planning and keeping track of a changing shape still matter. Check undo, restart and control repetition in the exact release. The appeal remains puzzle logic rather than rich character dialogue, and a player need not graduate to the original game to justify enjoying this one.
games.first: Complete or explore one introductory arrangement, focusing on how fruit changes the creature. Let curiosity about the next idea decide whether to continue.
games.ruling: The smaller rehearsal succeeds before the full costume returns. June's jacket history remains contested, and my best entrance cue turns out to be one finger from the front row.
games.source_note: Exact-title developer/publisher Steam description inspected for premise and edition. Fit and first trial are editorial suggestions. Controls, timing and comfort remain bounded by the explicit checks in the card; no complete playthrough performed.
games.quick_pitch: Try a gentler introduction to Snakebird's spatial idea, if a clearer opening challenge makes discovering its rules more appealing.
games.what_you_do: Work through the separate Primer game's introductory puzzles, moving the creature and learning how its shape affects each route.
games.watch_for: This is the easier separate game, not a guarantee of effortless puzzles; movement and undo still need checking.

games.title: A Good Snowman Is Hard To Build
games.case_title: The Snowman Had Better Posture Than the Host
scene: A Good Snowman Is Hard To Build made Kit fall in love with the idea of three rounded lanterns beside the signing table. I ordered them in gold.
Mika stacked the largest at the bottom. I suggested putting it on top for greater impact.
Rae stared at me. "Impact is exactly what I'm worried about."
The lanterns stayed in Mika's order. Remy added a little hat, and suddenly the decoration looked like a cheerful guest who had read the dress code.
June called it handsome. Dez said she had dated men with worse balance, then caught June laughing into her sleeve.
I gave the lantern guest my ceremonial sash. It wore the thing without complaining, moving, or requesting a speaking slot. Velvet suggested making it co-host.
"Nigga, I paid for him."
"And he's already doing less damage."
Shawna straightened my own jacket. We stood beside the finished arrangement for a photograph, two round-shouldered dignitaries of notably different competence.
games.pleasure: A Good Snowman Is Hard To Build makes a small, affectionate premise into a spatial puzzle: a monster creating snowmen. The compact scenes invite attention to a few objects and how their positions relate. It can offer a satisfying repeated activity without needing a sprawling world or a dense inventory story.
games.burden: The current developer listing declares play without timed input and keyboard-only support. Check movement, undo and snowball manipulation on the chosen device; those declarations do not establish that every action avoids holding. The puzzles still require planning and trial, so the gentle presentation should not become a promise of effortless solutions. Narrative is limited to the charm of the activity.
games.first: Try making one snowman and notice where your first plan changes. Learn the recovery control before treating a mistaken move as a reason to restart everything.

games.title: Tametsi
games.case_title: The Glitter Was Somewhere We Hadn't Counted
scene: Tametsi's careful deduction put Kit in a methodical mood just as Mika discovered loose glitter near the signing table. We needed to know which decorations were shedding before the papers arrived.
I suggested guessing.
Kit looked at me over her recovered glasses.
"That was a test," I said.
Rae inspected the garland. Remy checked his crown. Velvet shook her boa gently over a clean tray and proved, with some satisfaction, that the expensive feathers were innocent.
The trail led to my ceremonial sash. Every time I insisted on walking through the middle of the room, another little constellation appeared.
Mika replaced it with a plain ribbon. June brushed one last spark off Dez's sleeve and said the Blue Comet had never needed this much cleanup. Dez reminded her about the broken jukebox bulb.
Kit wrote the remaining checks on a card. We finished them one by one, and the table finally stopped looking as if it had hosted a tiny explosion.

games.title: Mario Paint
games.case_title: Mario Could Paint the Banner Faster Than My Committee
scene: Mario Paint's little creative tools persuaded Remy to design a simple welcome image instead of ordering another enormous photograph of me.
He made a microphone, a chair, and a bright uneven heart. Kit suggested clearer letters. Velvet requested enough sparkle in the drawing that we could stop shedding it in the room.
I asked where the host appeared.
Remy added a small crown on an empty chair.
"Nigga, that's a vacancy notice."
Shawna liked it. She said a welcome picture should leave room for people to arrive. Mika printed a draft at a sensible size, and Rae held it beside the entrance.
June and Dez argued over the heart's color, then both agreed the chair looked comfortable. Tank asked whether the microphone might also be a breadstick. Remy refused to settle the question.
The banner went up. For the first time all afternoon, somebody entering the room smiled before discovering how much I had spent.

games.title: Color a Dinosaur
games.case_title: The Dinosaur Got the First Uncontested Color
scene: Color a Dinosaur was a deliberately tiny activity, which made it perfect for settling our absurd argument over the rehearsal cards. Everyone wanted a different border color.
I announced a palette summit.
Rae said we were already at one and wanted dinner.
Dez chose green for the dinosaur picture on the screen. June said it suited him. The ease of this agreement stunned me so thoroughly that I tried to declare the old war over.
"Baby, we agreed on a dinosaur," June said.
Velvet laughed, then picked a border for her own cue card. Kit chose another. Mika added the same plain words to both, so the colors could differ without changing the meaning.
"Nigga," Tank said, "the animal got us farther than your speech."

I chose gold, naturally. Shawna let me, because my card was now small enough that the decision affected almost nobody else. Even decorative ambition improved when contained inside a reasonable rectangle.

games.title: The Incredible Machine 3
games.case_title: The Incredible Machine Was a Person Opening the Curtain
scene: The Incredible Machine 3's chain reactions encouraged me to sketch a ceremony opener involving a rolling ball, a tipping flag, and a bell that would release the curtain.
Rae stared at the page. "Who resets it?"
"An attendant."
"Then the attendant could open the curtain."

Remy liked the sketch anyway. He built a harmless tabletop demonstration with a marble and a little flag while the actual stage retained its ordinary pull. Kit watched the flag fall and applauded the tiny success.
Darnell arrived with a much more complicated proposal, a cocaine-party anecdote, and a yacht reference before reaching the second sentence. Mercedes pointed him toward the snack table.
"Nigga, take the long version somewhere with sandwiches."

Mika kept Remy's miniature machine in the display. It could amuse people without controlling the whole evening. Shawna asked me to pull the actual curtain once. I did. It opened beautifully, requiring neither a theory nor a marble to announce her entrance.

games.title: SimCity 2000 Special Edition
games.case_title: My City Had a Monument and No Toilets
scene: SimCity 2000 made planning a whole place look irresistible. I expanded our model ceremony into a miniature capital with a central monument, two plazas, and a boulevard named after Shawna.
She asked where the toilets were.
I explained that the capital was ceremonial.
"Nigga, so are a lot of emergencies."
Mika added the practical rooms and routes already agreed in the annex. Rae placed the food where it could be reached. Velvet put the dressing area near the stage instead of behind my monument.
The beautiful boulevard shrank. The place began working.
June examined the model and said her old bus route would never have cleared my original corner. Dez reminded her she had once clipped a flowerpot. June said the flowerpot had been badly governed.
Tank moved my monument to the small display table. I kept Shawna's name on the boulevard, now a very short route between our chairs and the courtyard. She approved its improved destination.

games.title: RollerCoaster Tycoon Deluxe
games.case_title: The Ride Was Two Chairs and My Big Mouth
scene: RollerCoaster Tycoon's park-building fantasy gave me a final dangerous thought: what if guests entered the signing ceremony on a little moving platform?
Mika's eyes lit up. Rae closed hers.
Velvet asked whether the platform could manage her costume. Kit asked whether it could simply remain still. Remy wanted to know if its fanfare came included.
The quotation arrived before we agreed to anything. That cured Mika.
"Nigga," Tank said, "we could pay everyone to walk."

June and Dez took two chairs at the front and began narrating the imaginary ride. June supplied the uphill anticipation. Dez supplied the terrible drop into my bank account. The entire room joined the scream.
I bowed as if I had commissioned the entertainment on purpose.

Shawna pulled me into the chair beside her. The actual floor did not move. Somebody brought drinks. I had to admit this attraction had remarkably good capacity, excellent comfort, and no additional installation fee.

games.title: Theme Hospital
games.case_title: The Hospital Admitted My Budget
scene: Theme Hospital's comic institution made Velvet declare an emergency consultation for our wounded ceremony budget. She seated me opposite her and asked where the spending hurt.
"Mostly in areas people haven't appreciated yet."
"Chronic," she said.

Rae brought the hardware receipts. Mika brought the revised layout. Kit carried one lamp that did the work of the three I had first ordered. Remy arrived as King Receipts with a clipboard and an appalling bedside pun.
"Nigga, don't operate on me with that joke."
We removed duplicate rentals, kept the technician's actual work, and paid Velvet's agreed fee without trying to cure it. The budget looked less feverish.
June said the Blue Comet had once balanced an entire evening with a coffee tin. Dez said June had forgotten who bought supper afterward.
Velvet handed back my pen. "Stable enough to stop ordering."
Shawna took the catalog from my other hand before I could challenge the discharge conditions.

games.title: Zoombinis
games.case_title: The Travelers Reached a Table That Finally Worked
scene: Zoombinis sent its travelers toward a new home through different reasoning problems. Our own procession faced the last rehearsal route: entrance, clear passage, chair, table, and a pen that actually wrote.
Mika invited people to try it in whatever order suited the check. Nobody had to perform the signing itself.
Kit reached her light. Velvet cleared the arch. Remy found his microphone. June and Dez sat together, still debating whether the Blue Comet jacket had been borrowed or strategically relocated.
Nia stopped beside Rae and asked if they could talk after the rehearsal. Rae smiled.
I lifted the charter, ready for a grand premature conclusion.
Shawna lowered my hand.
"Nigga, the room's ready. The words aren't."

We set the unsigned paper in its tray. The stage held everything it needed without requiring anyone to disappear into a role. Tank brought the last snacks over, and for once I announced nothing before taking one.
